indicators.indicator_source_text: Students connect their learning needs, strengths and interests to their goals and use technology to help achieve them and reflect on their progress.
met_criteria: Identifies specific personal learning strengths and gaps before selecting a goal
Sets a technology-mediated plan to work toward that goal with measurable steps
Actively reviews progress data or feedback and adjusts approach accordingly
Can articulate what they learned from a setback or feedback cycle
not_yet_met_criteria: Sets no personal learning goals; pursues assigned tasks only
Uses technology without connecting it to a learning purpose
Does not review or act on progress data or feedback
Cannot describe their own learning strengths or needs
partial_indicators: Tracks grades or completion but does not connect this to personal learning goals or reflection
Uses a tool because it is required, not because it serves a self-identified need
Reviews feedback after submission but does not change subsequent behaviour

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students build networks and customize their learning environments in ways that support the learning process.
met_criteria: Deliberately connects with peers, mentors, or online communities that support their learning
Customises digital tools, spaces, or workflows based on how they learn best
Uses their network as a learning resource, not just a social one
Revisits and updates their learning environment as needs change
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses default tool settings without customisation
Does not seek or maintain connections that support learning
Social digital networks are entirely separate from learning contexts
partial_indicators: Joins study groups or follows educational accounts but does not use these connections actively for learning
Customises aesthetics (themes, colour schemes) rather than functional learning-support features

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students use technology to seek feedback that informs and improves their practice and to demonstrate their learning in a variety of ways.
met_criteria: Actively seeks feedback using digital tools before a deadline
Uses multiple modalities to demonstrate learning (written, visual, audio, interactive)
Selects the demonstration format based on the audience and purpose, not just preference
Acts on feedback to produce a revised or improved output
not_yet_met_criteria: Waits for feedback to be provided without seeking it
Consistently uses the same format to demonstrate learning regardless of context
Does not revise work in response to feedback received
partial_indicators: Uses spell-check or grammar tools as feedback proxies but does not seek substantive formative feedback
Submits in an alternative format when explicitly offered one but does not initiate format choice

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students understand fundamental concepts of how technology works, demonstrate the ability to choose and use current technologies effectively, and are adept at thoughtfully exploring emerging technologies.
met_criteria: Can explain in plain terms how a digital tool works (e.g., why a search engine ranks results, how AI generates text)
Selects tools based on fitness for purpose rather than familiarity
Explores a new technology with curiosity and can evaluate its potential use
Recognises when a familiar tool is no longer the best fit and looks for alternatives
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses technology without any conceptual understanding of how it works
Always defaults to familiar tools regardless of whether they fit the task
Is reluctant or anxious about exploring unfamiliar technologies
partial_indicators: Can follow tutorials for new tools but cannot explain the underlying concepts
Tries new tools when directed to but does not independently seek or evaluate emerging options

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students manage their digital identity and understand the lasting impact of their online behaviors on themselves and others and make safe, legal and ethical decisions in the digital world.
met_criteria: Consciously curates their digital identity across platforms with awareness of lasting footprint
Can give examples of how online behaviour can have long-term consequences
Makes active choices about what to share, with whom, and on what platforms
Understands and applies legal and ethical standards in digital contexts (e.g., copyright, consent)
not_yet_met_criteria: Posts and interacts online without consideration of lasting impact
Has no awareness of digital footprint or identity management
Makes legal and ethical decisions based on 'everyone does it' rather than principles
partial_indicators: Uses a pseudonym or privacy setting on one platform but does not manage digital identity holistically
Knows about digital footprint as a concept but has not acted on it in their own practice

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students demonstrate empathetic, inclusive interactions online and use technology to responsibly contribute to their communities.
met_criteria: Actively creates inclusive online interactions, not just refraining from exclusion
Uses technology to make a positive contribution to a community (local or global)
Intervenes constructively when online interactions become harmful or exclusionary
Considers impact on others before posting or responding
not_yet_met_criteria: Engages online in ways that passively or actively exclude others
Uses technology for consumption rather than contribution
Does not intervene or act when harmful interactions occur in their online communities
partial_indicators: Is personally respectful online but does not actively champion inclusion or take action when others are excluded
Contributes positively within assigned platforms but not beyond required contexts

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students safeguard their well-being by being intentional about what they do online and how much time they spend online.
met_criteria: Makes active choices about online time use and has strategies to maintain healthy balance
Can identify when online activity is affecting wellbeing and takes corrective action
Distinguishes between purposeful and habitual digital engagement
Has personal norms for digital boundaries (e.g., offline time, notification management)
not_yet_met_criteria: Online time is unmonitored and habitual rather than intentional
Cannot identify connections between online behaviour and personal wellbeing
Has no strategies for managing digital engagement
partial_indicators: Is aware of screen time issues in general but has not developed personal strategies or norms
Uses wellbeing features on devices when prompted but not independently

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students take action to protect their digital privacy on devices and manage their personal data and security while online.
met_criteria: Reviews and adjusts privacy settings on new platforms before engaging
Understands what data is collected by tools they use and makes informed decisions
Uses security practices actively (strong passwords, two-factor authentication, reviewing permissions)
Can explain the difference between sharing, selling, and storing of personal data
not_yet_met_criteria: Accepts default privacy settings without review
Does not know what personal data is being collected by tools they use
Has no active security practices beyond basic password use
partial_indicators: Uses a strong password but does not review privacy settings or understand data collection practices
Knows data privacy is important but has not implemented any active management practices

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students use effective research strategies to find resources that support their learning needs, personal interests and creative pursuits.
met_criteria: Applies deliberate research strategies (Boolean operators, database filters, source type selection)
Adapts search strategy when initial results are insufficient
Locates domain-appropriate sources (e.g., academic databases for research, primary sources for history)
Can explain why a particular search strategy serves a given purpose
not_yet_met_criteria: Relies exclusively on a single search engine with basic keyword queries
Does not adapt strategy when searches do not yield useful results
Cannot articulate why they chose the sources they found
partial_indicators: Uses Google with some keyword variation but does not access specialist databases or apply systematic filters
Finds credible sources but by chance rather than deliberate strategy

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students evaluate the accuracy, validity, bias, origin, and relevance of digital content.
met_criteria: Examines author credentials, funding sources, and publication context
Identifies bias, perspective, and underlying assumptions in sources
Distinguishes between primary, secondary, and opinion sources
Cross-references claims across independent sources before accepting them
not_yet_met_criteria: Accepts content at face value if it comes from a familiar or visually credible website
Does not examine who produced content or why
Cannot distinguish opinion from evidence-based claims
partial_indicators: Checks whether a site is HTTPS or ends in .gov/.edu but does not examine author or funding
Looks for recent publication dates as the primary quality signal

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students curate information from digital resources using a variety of tools and methods to create collections of artifacts that demonstrate meaningful connections or conclusions.
met_criteria: Organises curated resources with annotations that explain connections between items
Uses curation tools purposefully to build collections that make an argument or represent a synthesis
Distinguishes curation from collection — the output demonstrates thinking, not just gathering
Can explain the logic or argument that their curated collection represents
not_yet_met_criteria: Saves links or copies content without annotation or synthesis
Cannot explain how the items in a collection relate to each other
Equates having more sources with doing more research
partial_indicators: Organises resources into labelled folders or categories but annotations are descriptive rather than analytical
Produces a bibliography rather than a curated collection that demonstrates constructed meaning

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students build knowledge by exploring real-world issues and gain experience in applying their learning in authentic settings.
met_criteria: Connects classroom learning to real-world problems or questions
Applies concepts in contexts beyond academic tasks
Engages with communities, data, or contexts outside school as part of their learning
Reflects on how their learning changes or informs their understanding of a real issue
not_yet_met_criteria: Treats learning as exclusively academic and does not seek real-world connections
Cannot explain how what they are learning applies outside the classroom
Does not engage with external communities or real-world data sources
partial_indicators: Mentions a real-world connection in a project but does not actually engage with the real-world context
Applies learning to a classroom simulation but not to an authentic external context

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students know and use a deliberate design process for generating ideas, testing theories, creating innovative artifacts or solving authentic problems.
met_criteria: Can name and follow a design process (e.g., design thinking, engineering design cycle)
Generates multiple ideas before selecting one, rather than implementing the first idea
Tests their design against criteria and revises based on results
Can articulate what each stage of the design process is for
not_yet_met_criteria: Moves directly from problem to solution without ideation or testing
Produces one idea and implements it without comparison or iteration
Cannot describe the steps they followed to arrive at their solution
partial_indicators: Knows the stages of a design process by name but does not apply them systematically in practice
Generates multiple ideas but selects based on preference rather than criteria

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students select and use digital tools to plan and manage a design process that considers design constraints and calculated risks.
met_criteria: Selects a digital planning tool appropriate to the complexity of the design project
Explicitly identifies constraints (time, materials, technical limits) and incorporates them in the plan
Assesses and accepts calculated risks in design decisions rather than avoiding all uncertainty
Uses the tool to track progress and make adjustments throughout the process
not_yet_met_criteria: Plans informally without a digital tool or structured approach
Does not identify or account for design constraints
Avoids risky or innovative choices to stay in the safety of the familiar
partial_indicators: Uses a project management tool for task tracking but does not use it to manage design constraints or assess risk
Identifies constraints after they become problems rather than anticipating them in planning

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students develop, test and refine prototypes as part of a cyclical design process.
met_criteria: Builds a prototype at an appropriate fidelity for the design stage
Tests the prototype with real users or against stated criteria, not just personal judgement
Uses test findings to make specific refinements to the prototype
Iterates at least twice before arriving at a final design
not_yet_met_criteria: Produces a final product without prototyping or testing
Tests only with themselves, not with end users or against external criteria
Does not revise after testing — treats the first prototype as the final version
partial_indicators: Builds a prototype and tests it with peers but treats their feedback as validation rather than input for revision
Revises surface features (appearance) rather than functional aspects identified through testing

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students exhibit a tolerance for ambiguity, perseverance and the capacity to work with open-ended problems.
met_criteria: Continues working productively when a problem has no single correct answer
Bounces back from setbacks and failed attempts without abandoning the project
Reframes constraints or unexpected findings as design opportunities rather than blockers
Can describe what they learned from a failed attempt
not_yet_met_criteria: Seeks a definitive answer or clear instruction before proceeding with open-ended tasks
Abandons or significantly truncates a project after the first major obstacle
Treats setbacks as evidence that the project cannot succeed
partial_indicators: Perseveres in the face of difficulty but seeks adult validation before continuing rather than exercising independent judgement
Accepts ambiguity in low-stakes tasks but not in assessed ones

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students formulate problem definitions suited for technology-assisted methods such as data analysis, abstract models and algorithmic thinking in exploring and finding solutions.
met_criteria: Identifies which aspects of a problem are suited to computational methods (data analysis, modelling, automation)
Reformulates a vague problem into a precise specification that a digital tool or algorithm could address
Distinguishes problems that benefit from computational approaches from those that do not
Uses abstraction to remove irrelevant detail before attempting a computational solution
not_yet_met_criteria: Approaches all problems the same way regardless of whether computational methods are appropriate
Cannot describe a problem in precise enough terms to be addressed computationally
Does not use abstraction — works with full complexity rather than building a model
partial_indicators: Identifies that a digital tool would help but does not reformulate the problem to fit computational methods
Uses abstraction by omitting detail without reasoning about which details matter

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students collect data or identify relevant data sets, use digital tools to analyze them, and represent data in various ways to facilitate problem-solving and decision-making.
met_criteria: Identifies appropriate datasets for a problem and assesses their quality and relevance
Uses digital tools to conduct meaningful analysis beyond basic charting
Chooses data representations suited to the question (not just the default chart type)
Draws and communicates conclusions from data analysis that inform decisions
not_yet_met_criteria: Collects or uses data without critical assessment of its relevance or quality
Produces visualisations without analytical interpretation
Cannot explain what the data shows or what decisions it supports
partial_indicators: Creates charts from data using default tool settings without explaining why a particular chart type was selected
Identifies a trend in data but cannot explain its implications for decision-making

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students break problems into component parts, extract key information, and develop descriptive models to understand complex systems or facilitate problem-solving.
met_criteria: Decomposes a complex problem into discrete, manageable sub-problems
Extracts only the information relevant to each sub-problem (abstraction)
Builds a model (diagram, flowchart, algorithm sketch) that captures the essential structure of the system
Uses the model to reason about the system before building or implementing a solution
not_yet_met_criteria: Attempts to solve complex problems as a whole without decomposition
Works with full information complexity without extracting what is relevant
Does not model systems — moves directly from problem to implementation
partial_indicators: Breaks a project into tasks on a to-do list but does not model the relationships between components or extract information
Draws a diagram of a system but uses it descriptively rather than to reason about the problem

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students understand how automation works and use algorithmic thinking to develop a sequence of steps to create and test automated solutions.
met_criteria: Can explain how an automated process works (inputs, outputs, conditional logic)
Develops a step-by-step algorithm to solve a problem before implementing it
Tests an automated solution against edge cases, not just the expected scenario
Identifies where automation is and is not appropriate in a given context
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses automated tools without understanding how they work
Cannot produce a step-by-step description of a solution process
Does not test automated solutions — assumes they work as intended
partial_indicators: Can record a macro or use automation features in a tool but cannot explain the underlying logic
Writes sequential steps but does not include conditional logic or test for varied inputs

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students choose the appropriate platforms and digital tools for meeting the desired objectives of their creation or communication.
met_criteria: Selects platforms based on the purpose, audience, and constraints of the communication
Can justify their platform choice with reference to the objective
Considers accessibility of the platform for the intended audience
Recognises when a chosen platform is not working and selects an alternative
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses the same platform regardless of purpose or audience
Cannot explain why they chose the platform they used
Does not consider whether their chosen platform is accessible to their audience
partial_indicators: Selects a different platform for each project but based on novelty or familiarity, not fitness for purpose
Considers audience but not platform affordances when making communication decisions

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students create original works or responsibly repurpose or remix digital resources into new creations.
met_criteria: Creates digital content that is original in design, argument, or creative expression
When remixing, transforms the source material significantly and acknowledges it correctly
Understands and applies relevant licensing and attribution norms (e.g., Creative Commons)
Can explain what makes their work original even when it builds on existing sources
not_yet_met_criteria: Reproduces existing content with minimal or no modification
Does not attribute sources or understand attribution requirements
Cannot distinguish between reproducing, remixing, and creating
partial_indicators: Attributes sources correctly but does not transform them — the work is a collage rather than a synthesis
Changes aesthetics (colour, layout) of existing work without substantive transformation of content or argument

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students use digital tools to visually communicate complex ideas to others.
met_criteria: Selects visual representation methods suited to the complexity and type of the idea
Produces visualisations that aid understanding rather than just illustrating what is already stated
Uses data visualisation, diagram, or interactive media to make a complex idea accessible
Can explain the design decisions behind their visual communication choices
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses default slide templates or generic images that do not aid comprehension
Cannot explain why they chose a particular visual format
Visual elements are decorative rather than communicative
partial_indicators: Creates a chart or diagram that accurately represents the data but does not explain what it means for the audience
Produces visually polished outputs that simplify rather than communicate complex ideas

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students publish or present content that customizes the message and medium for their intended audiences.
met_criteria: Adapts both content and medium for each distinct audience
Can articulate how the same core message requires different treatment for different audiences
Considers how the audience will access and engage with the content when selecting the medium
Seeks or incorporates feedback from the intended audience to refine the communication
not_yet_met_criteria: Presents or publishes the same content in the same format regardless of audience
Adapts language informally but does not reconsider medium or structure
Does not account for how different audiences will actually encounter the content
partial_indicators: Simplifies language for a different audience but uses the same medium and format
Creates audience-specific versions when explicitly required but not independently

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students use digital tools to connect with peers from a variety of backgrounds, recognizing diverse viewpoints and broadening mutual understanding.
met_criteria: Actively seeks connections with peers from different cultural, geographic, or social backgrounds
Uses digital tools purposefully to create these connections, not just to find information about different groups
Engages in genuine dialogue that leads to perspective shift or deepened understanding
Reflects on how diverse perspectives have changed or enriched their own thinking
not_yet_met_criteria: Collaborates only within their immediate peer group
Reads about diverse perspectives without engaging with people who hold them
Does not use digital tools to build cross-cultural connections
partial_indicators: Reads sources from different cultural contexts but does not use collaborative tools to engage directly with people from those contexts
Participates in a global online community but in a passive (comment, lurk) rather than connective way

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students use collaborative technologies to work with others, including peers, experts or community members, to examine issues and problems from multiple viewpoints.
met_criteria: Uses collaborative tools (shared documents, video conferencing, discussion forums) to work with people outside their immediate context
Brings multiple viewpoints into the analysis of a problem rather than seeking confirmation
Engages with experts or community members — not just peer groups — using technology
Synthesises different perspectives into a more complete understanding of an issue
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses technology for one-way information gathering rather than collaborative examination
Does not seek or engage with viewpoints that challenge their existing perspective
Collaboration is limited to familiar peers
partial_indicators: Participates in a collaborative technology activity but does not seek out or synthesise multiple viewpoints within it
Connects with people from different contexts but uses the connection for information, not collaborative inquiry

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students contribute constructively to project teams, assuming various roles and responsibilities to work effectively toward a common goal.
met_criteria: Takes on different roles across projects rather than always defaulting to one contribution type
Contributes in ways that actively move the team toward its goal, not just complete a personal task
Supports other team members and helps resolve disagreements constructively
Reflects on their contribution and adjusts it based on what the team needs
not_yet_met_criteria: Always takes the same role in team tasks
Completes their own portion without regard for the team's overall progress
Does not engage with team dynamics or support other members
partial_indicators: Completes assigned tasks reliably but does not flex roles, support others, or contribute beyond their designated scope
Takes on a leadership role when available but does not contribute constructively in supporting roles

indicators.indicator_source_text: Students explore local and global issues, and use collaborative technologies to work with others to investigate solutions.
met_criteria: Identifies a real local or global issue that they explore as part of their learning
Uses collaborative technology to investigate the issue with partners outside their immediate context
Co-develops or evaluates potential solutions collaboratively rather than independently
Connects local and global dimensions of the issue in their analysis
not_yet_met_criteria: Studies issues as text-based academic topics without connecting them to the real world
Does not use collaborative technology to investigate or co-develop solutions
Analysis is individually produced without external collaborative input
partial_indicators: Researches a global issue and discusses it in class but does not use collaborative technology to work with partners outside school
Uses collaborative tools to communicate with peers about an issue but produces an individual rather than genuinely co-created analysis
